Q136297107.summary: Beneath an arched canopy and a hanging curtain, a tall Christ, identified as IC XC, stands on a footstool and lays his hands on the crowned heads of the Emperor Otto II and the Empress Theophanu, who stand in richly patterned robes on either side. A small figure kneels at the emperor's feet, and inscriptions in a mixture of Greek and Latin letters name the imperial pair. Closely modelled on Byzantine coronation ivories, the plaque proclaims that earthly rulers receive their authority from Christ.
facts: The Musée de Cluny's ivory was produced in the German empire in 982–983 in a Byzantine-inspired style, according to the French Wikipedia article on the museum.
Theophanu, a Byzantine princess, married Otto II in Rome in April 972 and was crowned empress the same day; Otto II died in December 983.
Byzantine ivories of the so-called Romanos group, such as the Romanos and Eudokia plaque in Paris, show Christ crowning an emperor and empress in just this way.
Q136297107.notes: Inv. Cl. 392. The kneeling figure is often identified as a monk named John (probably John Philagathos), but this was seen only in a search-result summary and is not asserted here. The place of carving (Germany, northern Italy) is debated.
Q136297107.original_title: Le Christ couronnant Otton II et Théophano

cur:manuscripts-egberti-blind-jericho.summary: Followed by apostles, Christ reaches out to a blind man sitting by the roadside with his staff; a tree with mushroom-like foliage and the label 'caecus' (blind man) complete the scene.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.
During the Second World War the codex was evacuated to Giessen University Library, survived its bombing in December 1944, and was brought back to Trier in May 1945 from a parsonage at Elkerhausen.

cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-descent-in.summary: Beneath an arch at the top of the page, a haloed Christ grasps the hand of a naked figure rising from the dark pit, with a second haloed figure beside him and the broken doors of hell flung through the air at the left. Below, in a brown abyss, crowds of naked souls are tormented by demons around a dark, bound figure — Satan in chains. The image shows Christ's victory over death and his liberation of the righteous dead.
facts: Unlike most Beatus manuscripts, the Girona copy opens with a cycle of pictures of the life and Passion of Christ before the commentary on the Apocalypse.

The Girona Beatus was completed on 6 July 975 for an abbot Dominicus, probably at the monastery of Tábara; unusually, its painters are named: 'Ende, woman painter and servant of God', and the monk-priest Emeterius.
cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-descent-in.notes: Commons titles this page simply 'Hell' (fol. 17v). The identification of the upper scene as Christ freeing Adam from hell is based on the visible broken doors and the haloed figure leading a naked man upward.

cur:manuscripts-leon-bible-960-christ-in.summary: Within an ornamental frame of interlace, Christ sits in a central medallion, haloed and blessing, holding a book; around him, linked by a vine-like lattice, four medallions hold the winged symbols of the evangelists, each with a book. The page opens the Bible with an image of Christ proclaimed by the four Gospels.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the Bible begins with this full-page image of Christ and the four evangelist symbols, followed by ten pages of tables tracing Christ's descent from Adam and Eve.
Its colophon records completion at Valeránica on 19 June 960 by the scribe Sanctus and his master Florentius, who are shown toasting the finished work beneath a great omega on fol. 514r.
